Q: Select datetime columns in Polars A:

You can select polars columns by datatypes as you did with pl.String, but you have to pass a polars datatype to make that work, not a python datetime.datetime value/object.

Below we select all datetime datatypes that have "us" resolution by passing the pl.Datetime("us") datatype.

import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime

df_trades = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "time1": [
            datetime(2020, 1, 1, 9, 1, 0),
            datetime(2020, 1, 1, 9, 1, 0),
            datetime(2020, 1, 1, 9, 3, 0),
            datetime(2020, 1, 1, 9, 6, 0),
        ],
        "time2": [
            datetime(2020, 1, 1, 9, 1, 0),
            datetime(2020, 1, 1, 9, 1, 0),
            datetime(2020, 1, 1, 9, 3, 0),
            datetime(2020, 1, 1, 9, 6, 0),
        ],
        "stock": ["A", "B", "B", "C"],
        "trade": [101, 299, 301, 500],
    }
)

df_trades.select(
    pl.col(pl.Datetime("us"))
)

shape: (4, 2)
┌─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┐
│ time1               ┆ time2               │
│ ---                 ┆ ---                 │
│ datetime[μs]        ┆ datetime[μs]        │
╞═════════════════════╪═════════════════════╡
│ 2020-01-01 09:01:00 ┆ 2020-01-01 09:01:00 │
│ 2020-01-01 09:01:00 ┆ 2020-01-01 09:01:00 │
│ 2020-01-01 09:03:00 ┆ 2020-01-01 09:03:00 │
│ 2020-01-01 09:06:00 ┆ 2020-01-01 09:06:00 │
└─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┘

Q: Polars - with_columns on columns that end in a "D" and are of type datetime A:

You could use selectors:

import polars.selectors as cs

df.with_columns(cs.datetime() & cs.ends_with('D'))

# or
df.with_columns(cs.datetime() & cs.matches('^.+D$'))

Selectors support set operations such as:

UNION: A | B

INTERSECTION: A & B

DIFFERENCE: A - B

COMPLEMENT: ~A

Q: Cast columns that might not exist in Polars A:

You can use column selectors to select columns by name with pl.selectors.by_name and pass require_all=False.

import polars.selectors as cs

df.with_columns(
    cs.by_name(columns_to_cast, require_all=False).cast(pl.Float64)
)

Q: How to turn a list of Polars expressions into one multi-column expression? A:

You can do:

powers_expr =pl.col([x.meta.output_name() for x in powers_list])

or you can make it a function and monkey patch it in like

def toexpr(list_in):
    return pl.col([x.meta.output_name() for x in list_in])
pl.to_expr=toexpr
### Now this works
powers_expr = pl.to_expr(powers_list)

then

df.with_columns(powers_expr + 10)
shape: (3, 6)

Q: mongodb.conf bind_ip = 127.0.0.1 does not work, but 0.0.0.0 works A:

When the setting is bindIp: 127.0.0.1 (or bindIp: localhost), then mongod listens only to the loopback IP address. This means you can connect only from the local machine where mongod is running.

When the setting is bindIp: 0.0.0.0 (or bindIpAll: true), then mongod listens to all IP addresses. This means you can connect from any remote computer, unless the connection is blocked by your firewall.

Note, localhost is an alias which may resolve to the IPv4 address 127.0.0.1 or to the IPv6 address ::1. See Can't connect to MongoDB 6.0 Server locally using Node.js driver.

Apart from all that, authentication should be always enabled, without any exception, period!

Q: Aggregating time and space dependent data efficiently A:

Why not add a step where you quantize the time to the desired granularity, and then dplyr::summarize(..., .by = c(ID, period)) for the three functions? This seems like a straightforward summarization, what am I missing?

(See https://stackoverflow.com/search?q=%5Br%5D+group+by+time for many similar questions that aggregate data by time period.)

library(dplyr); library(lubridate)
my_agg <- \(x, period = "day") {
  x |>
    mutate(period = floor_date(datetime, period)) |>
    summarize(TMin = min(TMin), 
              TMax = max(TMax),
              TMean = mean(TMean),
              .by = c(ID, period))
}
